As of 315 AM EDT Tuesday...

KEY MESSAGE 1...Rain is expected to become more widespread today as 
a front lingers across the area. 

Early morning surface analysis shows a broad area of high pressure 
over Ontario, Canada extending outwards into New England and 
portions of the Mid-Atlantic. The cold front that passed through our 
area today is currently draped across central and southern NC. Low 
cloud cover persists across the CWA with showers moving along the 
northern boundary across northern VA and portions of the MD Eastern 
Shore. Rain is expected to become more widespread later this morning 
as the front lifts back north. Exact coverage and timing of the
rain has a slightly lower confidence, but today will have the 
best rain chances of the last few days. Some isolated 
thunderstorms can't be totally ruled out for the southern half 
of the area, which could lead to heavy downpours and localized 
flash flooding. A couple of efficient storms along the NC/VA 
border into NE NC last evening produced 2-3" of rain in a short 
period, which even caused over a foot of rise on the Cashie 
River in Windsor. Expect the same efficient rainfall makers to 
be possible again today. WPC has a Slight Risk of Excessive 
Rainfall for the southeast half of the CWA, excluding the SE VA 
and NE NC coast. 

Additionally, northeast winds will increase later this morning as 
the Canadian high pressure shifts east and low pressure forms off 
the NC/SC coast. Locations along the coast, including the entire 
Eastern Shore, Norfolk, Hampton Roads, and into Currituck County 
will see wind gusts upwards of 25-30mph by this afternoon. The 
Atlantic coast of the Eastern Shore including Ocean City and 
Chincoteague will see their gusts build to 40-45mph overnight. These 
higher gusts will persist for the coastline through Thursday night. 
Further inland, gusts to ~20mph are expected starting this 
afternoon. High temperatures will be noticeably cooler for most of 
the area today as the cooler airmass works its way in from the 
north. High temperatures will range from the upper 60s across the 
north to the lower 80s along the south. Lows tonight will dip into 
the upper 50s for our western counties, with upper 60s for the 
southeast.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Strong onshore flow, cooler temperatures, and
rainy conditions will continue on Wednesday. Rain chances 
gradually shift east Thursday, potentially making for a dry end
to the week. Gusty winds will persist. 

Cold air damming will overtake the area on Wednesday as high 
pressure remains parked to our north. This will make for our coolest 
day of the week as high temperatures top out in the low to mid 60s 
for the western and northern inland areas, with low 70s for the SE 
half of the CWA. Inland gusts to 20mph are forecast through the
day. Winds for coastal counties will persistently be blowing 
around 20-25mph with gusts to 35+mph. The strongest winds will 
continue to be along the Atlantic coast with gusts to 40-45mph 
expanding down the span of our coastline through the day on 
Wednesday. These winds are forecast to stick around through 
Thursday night as the tightened pressure gradient between the 
strong high pressure to the north and the strengthening low 
pressure over the ocean remains. This persistent onshore flow 
will create really rough beach conditions, as high surf/wave 
heights and beach erosion are likely. Wednesday will also be 
when moderate to locally major coastal flooding starts, so if 
you live in a coastal zone, please read our tidal flooding 
section below and stay tuned to the latest forecasts. With the 
CAD wedge in place, the environment will be stable leading to 
steady stratiform rain across the area. While it won't have the 
higher intensity rates of a thunderstorm (since we will be too 
capped for those), the persistent rainfall could still create 
some flooding concerns. Lows will cool off a few more degrees 
Wednesday night with low to mid 50s inland and low 60s east. 

Rain chances then look to become more confined to eastern portions 
of the area Thursday into the first part of Friday as a secondary 
surface low forms along our coast and causes the main low to deepen, 
as well as finally have the potential to gain some forward momentum. 
Models disagree on exactly where the low will be on Friday, 
with the GFS moving it off to the northeast while the ECMWF 
keeps it closer to our shore. One solution will allow for winds 
to subside later Friday and drier air to move in for the 
weekend, while the other keeps the elevated impactful conditions
lingering a bit longer. For now, went with rain chances ending 
Friday making way for a mostly dry weekend. Winds will likely
shift to be more N/NW overnight Thursday into Friday. This will
allow speeds to subside a bit, but gusts to 25-30mph may still 
be possible into the weekend.
